title: Close interbreeding lowers fertility while occasional crossing raises it

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Close interbreeding lowers fertility while occasional crossing raises it

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Close interbreeding lessens fertility, while an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases it; this explains much of the declining fertility of hybrids kept for successive generations.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: that close interbreeding lessens fertility, and, on the other hand, that an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases fertility

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VIII, “Hybridism”; section “Sterility various in degree, not universal, affected by close interbreeding, removed by domestication”. Scope: plants and animals, including hybrids bred over several generations

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch08-02: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Inbreeding depression and heterosis are directly measurable with many public pedigrees and experiments. Standard mixed models can resolve the broad directional claim while testing alternative hybrid mechanisms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Model fertility and offspring viability against pedigree inbreeding coefficients and genetic distance of mates, including hybrid lineages across generations. Decline under close inbreeding and recovery after outcrossing support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Effects vary among taxa and genetic backgrounds.

Hybrid decline can also reflect segregation and incompatibilities.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fertility and inbreeding coefficient are measured together in more than one public pedigree, and the decision rule is a standard regression that a small team can run quickly. The same negative relationship is widely tabulated for other animals and for plants, so the stated generality is not hanging on one species. What the datasets do not settle is Darwin's use of the pattern to explain multi-generation hybrid decline in particular.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress fertility or offspring number on pedigree or genomic inbreeding coefficient, treating low inbreeding as the occasional cross with a less related mate. A negative slope confirms that closer interbreeding lowers fertility and that less related matings raise it; a flat or positive slope would refute the relationship.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
These open pedigrees are animals; plant inbreeding-depression tables are more scattered.

Environmental stress changes the slope, so a single population is not the whole relationship.

The further application to hybrids kept for several generations is not the design of these wild pedigrees.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If close interbreeding lessens fertility and an occasional cross with a distinct stock increases it, then (i) in a pedigreed wild mammal population, litter size should decline with the mother's inbreeding coefficient, and (ii) in experimentally inbred Drosophila populations, fecundity should be lower than in the outbred control and should rise again when individuals from different inbred populations are crossed (heterosis).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Bear: ordinary least-squares regression of litter size on the mother's pedigree inbreeding coefficient over 66 litters (29 mothers), one-sided test for a negative slope; the litter's own inbreeding coefficient and mother-level means are reported as extras. Fly: the DATA sheet of the Dryad workbook was parsed; offspring fecundity ('F eggs per vial') of within-population random crosses (type 1) in the inbred treatments was compared with the outbred control, and inter-population crosses (type 2) were compared with within-population crosses in each population-size x generation cell (relative heterosis), plus a pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney test.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Dataset 1 (Auclair et al. 2025, Pyrenean brown bear, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.w9ghx3g1s, file litter_size_dt.csv): the slope of litter size on maternal inbreeding coefficient (ordinary least squares, one row per litter; if the file supplies repeated mothers, a mother-level mean is also reported) is negative with one-sided p < 0.05, or, if the coefficient is categorical, mean litter size of the most inbred category is below that of the least inbred with p < 0.05. Dataset 2 (Pekkala et al. 2014, Drosophila littoralis, Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.10154): (a) mean fecundity of inbred populations is below the outbred control in at least two of the three population-size treatments (N = 2, 10, 40), and (b) mean fecundity of inter-population crosses exceeds that of within-population matings (heterosis > 0) in a majority of population pairs or treatments for which both are reported. Verdict 'supports' if dataset 1 passes and both 2(a) and 2(b) pass; 'mixed' if dataset 1 passes but only one of 2(a)/2(b), or dataset 1 fails while both 2(a) and 2(b) pass; 'refutes' if litter size does not decline with inbreeding and inbred fecundity is not below control.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refuted if the litter-size slope on inbreeding is >= 0 (or not significantly negative) and inbred Drosophila populations are not less fecund than the outbred control. Clause (ii)(b) failing alone (no heterosis) with the others passing gives 'mixed'. If either Dryad archive cannot be downloaded, that dataset is recorded as unavailable and the verdict rests on the other; if neither can be obtained, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: cubs per litter per unit maternal inbreeding coefficient (OLS slope)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'close interbreeding lessens fertility' is read as inbreeding depression in a fertility component (litter size in a wild mammal; fecundity in a laboratory fly), and 'an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases it' as heterosis on crossing distinct inbred populations. The inbreeding coefficient (Wright's F) is a post-Darwinian quantity. The clause attributing the decline of multi-generation hybrids to close interbreeding is not tested; only the general inbreeding-depression and heterosis pattern is. Exact column names and the form of the inbreeding variable were not inspected before pre-registration; the mapping used is stated in 'method'.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Data from: Inbreeding depression across multiple life history traits in a long-lived mammal (Pyrenean brown bear), file litter_size_dt.csv

Data from: The effect of inbreeding rate on fitness, inbreeding depression and heterosis over a range of inbreeding coefficients (Drosophila littoralis)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The pre-registered bear test is marginal (one-sided p = 0.044, n = 66 litters); the litter's own inbreeding coefficient gives a clearer signal (p = 0.001). In the fly data the N = 40 treatment was not less fecund than the N = 500 control, so inbreeding depression in fecundity appears only at the two smallest population sizes, although fecundity declines significantly with the estimated inbreeding coefficient overall.

Two datasets only (one wild mammal population of a few dozen mothers; one laboratory Drosophila experiment); Darwin's claim is about plants and animals generally.

The pre-registered bear test uses the mother's inbreeding coefficient; the litter's own coefficient (closeness of the parents) is the more literal reading of 'close interbreeding' and is reported as an extra.

Bear litter sizes are counts (1-3) observed in the field; detection delay and maternal age are confounders that the simple regression does not model (the source paper fits mixed models with these covariates).

In the fly experiment 'distinct variety' is another inbred laboratory population of the same species, not a distinct variety in Darwin's sense; heterosis there reflects complementation of different fixed deleterious alleles.

The clause attributing the decline of hybrids over generations to close interbreeding is not tested.
